# Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates **_Abstract_--Production vector search must continuously ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high- recall, metadata-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries for many tenants with per-tenant service-level objectives. Existing graph-based ANN systems address these requirements largely in isolation, leaving recall during concurrent re- optimization without an analytical bound. We develop a graph- based index that combines streaming updates, filtered search, and multi-tenancy, with one theoretical result and two system mechanisms. Our theory decomposes per-tenant recall loss into staleness from updates not yet integrated into the graph and filtered navigability determined by the local density of points satisfying a tenant’s predicate. The staleness component exhibits anti-amortization on a merge-based graph, integrating a larger batch of inserts increases recall degradation super-linearly, so larger merges do not reduce total staleness loss. Holding the insert horizon fixed while increasing merge size \(20\times\), we observe a monotonic decrease in terminal recall@10 from 99.44% to 99.01%. For filtered search, the theory gives a parameter-free frontier-mass relationship in local predicate density and a query- averaged per-tenant recall bound. We instantiate the bound with a filter and tenant-aware staging cache and a select-not-resize scheduler with per-tenant staleness ceilings. On a FreshDiskANN substrate, the ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under the evaluated churn workload, while merge reordering changes terminal recall by only 0.02 percentage points. The results show how recall bounds can guide background maintenance without relying on merge resizing as a recall control mechanism.** **_Index Terms_--Approximate nearest neighbor search, vector databases, graph indexes, streaming indexes, filtered search, multi-tenancy, recall, service-level objectives, index maintenance, concurrent updates.** ### I. INTRODUCTION A WIDELY-HELD intuition about maintaining a graph- based approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) index under a stream of inserts is that batching amortizes cost, since folding more pending points into each merge lowers per-point maintenance overhead. This holds for _throughput_; for _recall_ it does not. Integrating a batch of _c_ inserts into a merge-based graph index degrades disk-graph recall@_k super-linearly_ in _c_, so the total recall loss accumulated over an insertion horizon does not fall with the merge size. Larger, less frequent merges are no better for recall than smaller, more frequent ones, and on our point estimates they are worse. We call this _anti- amortization_. In practice only the weak form matters, since re-sizing merges cannot engineer degradation away and can only _re-prioritize_ it, and this motivates the system we build. The design rests on the _direction_ of the effect (_L_∗ non- decreasing in _c_), which we measure on two independent axes; the magnitude of the super-linearity is less tightly pinned, and its per-merge-to-horizon assembly is a conservative step we find loose by about \(2\times\) (§V-B). Anti-amortization matters because the workloads that most need graph ANN are exactly the ones that mutate continuously. Production vector search must ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high-recall queries that carry metadata predicates, for many tenants each with its own service-level objective (SLO). Recent work names the pain directly. CANDOR-Bench [1] observes that under concurrency "throughput in concurrent settings is often constrained by insertion overhead rather than query latency, which highlights a mismatch between streaming workloads and designs originally tuned for offline construction." The VDBMS Survey [2] places incremental _k_-NN among its open problems: e-commerce and recommender platforms retrieve an effectively very large _k_ in small increments so that results appear seamlessly, and while techniques exist for that access pattern, "it is unclear how to support this search inside vector indexes." A VLDB tutorial on filtered vector search [3] makes the corresponding point on the predicate axis, giving as a key objective "the importance of achieving stable recall, ideally in a declarative manner, ensuring consistent recall across queries." And, from industry, Pinecone [4] reports that "data is continuously inserted and deleted, and metadata may be updated independently of the vector index, yet filters must be applied accurately and efficiently at query time." The literature is heavily worked along each axis _separately_ but not at their intersection. Filtered-static graph ANN (Filtered-DiskANN, ACORN, RNSG, iRangeGraph, STABLE) builds one index over the joint feature-and- attribute space and does not stream. Streaming graph ANN (FreshDiskANN, SPFresh, Mycelium-Index, and the recent single-tenant SOTA PipeANN/OdinANN) operates on unfiltered, single-tenant data and provides at best _empirical_ recall stability under churn. Multi-tenant vector search (Curator, Pinecone, GaussDB-Vector) is sparse; Curator is static and in- memory, Pinecone sits on an IVF substrate with no analytical bound, and none schedules background work by per-tenant SLA. No prior system occupies their intersection, and none bounds the recall a tenant loses during live re-optimization of a filtered graph index. Our contribution occupies the axes those systems leave open, combining streaming, filtered, and multi-tenant operation with per-tenant SLA scheduling, an analytical bound, and disk-resident scale. On the axes they do target, PipeANN and OdinANN lead single-tenant streaming and Curator leads static per-tenant recall, and we position against rather than Namrata Das, Kailas Devadkar, Anand Godbole
Sardar Patel Institute of Technology, Mumbai, India

We make one theoretical and two engineering contributions. Our theorem (C1, §III) establishes the anti-amortization bound and generalizes it to the filtered, multi-tenant, deletes/migration setting. Its filtered term is a _parameter- free_ frontier-mass law in the _local_ predicate density \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) that predicts the recovery scale \(L_{95}=1.25k/\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) and yields a per-tenant admission test \(1.25k/\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\le L_\mathrm{max}(\ell_\tau)\); evaluated as a query average, it is a conservative per-tenant recall lower bound. The staleness half is measured at horizon scale rather than extrapolated, with terminal recall decreasing monotonically as the merge size grows across a \(20\times\) range of _c_.

Two engineering designs instantiate the bound. A filter and tenant-aware staging cache (C2, §IV) absorbs in-flight inserts, deletes, and tenancy changes on the query path and collapses to the baseline on a single partition. An SLA- aware, select-not-resize scheduler (C3) honors a per-tenant max-staleness ceiling, re-prioritizing which pending work each fixed-size merge drains rather than re-sizing the merge that anti-amortization forbids.

On a FreshDiskANN substrate we measure that anti- amortization holds end to end (at a fixed 60K-insert horizon, terminal recall@10 falls \(99.44\rightarrow 99.01\) as merges grow \(1\text{K}\rightarrow 20\text{K}\)), that re-ordering merges leaves terminal recall unchanged (\(|\Delta\text{recall@10}|=0.02\) pp), that the per-tenant staleness ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under churn where a ceiling-less baseline fails, and that the design remains memory-bounded and recall-correct at 100K.

## II. SYSTEM MODEL AND NOTATION

### _Vectors, queries, predicates_

Let \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be the ambient space with metric \(\rho\). A point \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) carries metadata \(m(x)\in\mathcal{M}\); a _predicate_ \(p:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\{0,1\}\) selects the filtered subset X_<sub>p</sub>_={_x:p(m(x_))=1}, of _global selectivity_ \(\sigma(p)=|\mathcal{X}_p|/|\mathcal{X}|\). A _query_ is _q_=(_v,k,p_) with query vector _v_, neighbor count _k_, and predicate _p_; its ground truth is the _k_ closest points of X_<sub>p</sub>_ to _v_ under \(\rho\). Because filtered-graph recall is governed by predicate density _near the query_ rather than globally (§III), we also define the query- joint _local density_ \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(p,v)=\mathrm{Pr}_{x\sim\mathrm{nbhd}(v)}[p(m(x))=1]\), the fraction of _v_’s metric neighborhood that satisfies _p_.

### _Tenants and SLOs_

The point set is marked by tenant: T is the tenant set and \(t(x)\in\mathcal{T}\) each point’s tenant. A query has tenant scope \(T(q)\subseteq\mathcal{T}\) (single-tenant when |_T(q_)|=1); its effective candidate set is \(\mathcal{X}_p\cap\{x:t(x)\in T(q)\}\). Each tenant \(\tau\) carries a service-level objective \(\text{SLO}(\tau)=(\rho_\tau,\ell_\tau)\) (minimum recall \(\rho_\tau\), maximum latency \(\ell_\tau\)) and a _max-staleness ceiling_ \(S_\tau\) that the scheduler (§IV) honors.

### _Graph index_

_G_=(_V,E_) is a directed graph over \(V\subseteq\mathcal{X}\) built by Yamana (out-degree cap _R_, candidate width _L_, prune slack \(\alpha>1\), pool cap `maxc`); Search(_G,q,ef_) returns an approximate top-_k_ using exploration budget _ef_. **The disk graph is a**<tbc>

<tbc>**single _label-blind_ Yamana:** predicates and tenant labels are query-time post-filter tags and are never used in construction. This fact is central to both the theorem’s additivity and topology preservation (§III,§IV).

### _Mutation streams_

Updates arrive as a marked point process _M_={(_s<sub>i</sub>,u<sub>i</sub>_)} with \(u_i\in\{\mathrm{ins}(x),\mathrm{del}(x),\mathrm{mig}(x,\tau\rightarrow\tau')\}\) and per-class rates \(\lambda_\mathrm{ins},\lambda_\mathrm{del},\lambda_\mathrm{mig}\). The toy setting (§III) is Poisson inserts-only (\(\lambda_\mathrm{del}=\lambda_\mathrm{mig}=0\)); the general theorem admits all three (migration = a delete in \(\tau\) plus an insert in \(\tau'\)).

### _Cache, scheduler, compaction_

A filter-aware, tenant-aware _staging cache C_ of capacity _c_ holds pending mutations and is consulted on the query path, keyed by (_p,T(q_)). A priority-queue _scheduler_ orders background graph-repair work by a composite key \(\kappa=\alpha_1\mathrm{stale}+\alpha_2\widehat{\Delta R}+\alpha_3\mathrm{SLA}+\alpha_4\mathrm{mig}\). Compaction fires a merge when cache occupancy reaches _c_ (the theorem’s referent for _c_); the merge integrates the pending batch into _G_ and resets the cache.

### _Recall as a random variable_

For query _q_ at time _t_, \(R_q(t)=|(\text{Search}(G_t,q,ef)\cup\text{Cache}_t(q))\cap\mathrm{GT}(q,t)|/k\). The _per-tenant recall_ is \(\bar{R}_\tau(t)=\mathbb{E}_q[R_q(t)|T(q)\unknown\tau]\), and the _recall@k loss_ is \(L_\tau(t)=\rho_\tau-\bar{R}_\tau(t)\). The object the theorem bounds is the worst-case _over time_ of the query-averaged per-tenant loss on the horizon \[0_,T_\], \(L_\tau^*=\mathrm{sup}_{t\in[0,T]}L_\tau(t)\): worst-case in _t_, in expectation over _q_, so the guarantee is on the query average rather than on any individual query.

## III. THE RECALL-BOUNDED STALENESS THEOREM (C1)

We first prove the central kernel in the toy setting (single tenant, no filter, inserts only), then lift it to the filtered, multi- tenant, deletes/migration setting. The staleness half of the bound is _semi-empirical / loose-but-correct-form_: its mechanism and functional shape are derived and validated on two independent axes, while the exponents are calibrated. The filtered half is derived and parameter-free. We state this status precisely throughout.

### A. The toy bound: anti-amortization

**Definition 1** (Batch-merge operator M_<sub>c</sub>_)**.** Let _G_<sub>0</sub> be the disk graph over _N_ points and _B_ a batch of _c_ pending inserts. M_<sub>c</sub>(G_<sub>0</sub>_,B_) acts in two phases. _Forward_: each \(x\in B\) obtains out-neighbors by greedy search against the _frozen_ snapshot _G_<sub>0</sub> then ROBUSTPRUNE/\(\alpha\)-RNG to degree _R_; _G_<sub>0</sub> is not mutated during the batch. _Reconcile_: each existing node unions its buffered reverse edges and re-prunes (on PQ distances) only if it exceeds _R_. Two structural consequences follow: (M1) the _c_ batch points are _mutually invisible_ during selection (no \(x\in B\) takes another batch point as a neighbor, unlike a from-scratch build); (M2) hubs flooded by batch reverse edges are re-pruned tossily on approximate distances.

<tbc>**Assumption 2** (Empirical per-merge degradation model, calibrated on this substrate)**.** Integrating one batch of _c_ inserts via M_<sub>c</sub>_ into _G_<sub>0</sub> (over _N_ points) reduces expected disk-graph recall@_k_, relative to a from-scratch \(\alpha\)-RNG build on the same final set, by

\(g(c,N)=min\big(g_0(L)+\Theta\big(min(c^2/N,Rc)^\psi\big),\frac{c}{N+c}\big),\) (1)

the **batch term** (M1, super-linear in _c_; _R_-cap-limited, lifted near-linearly \(\psi\approx 1\) to recall) plus a small budget-soft _V_<sub>0</sub> **floor** _g_<sub>0</sub>(_L_) (M2), capped by the batch fraction.

_Calibration (full fits, sample sizes and diagnostics in §V-B)._ The exponent is fit on two independent axes that must not be conflated. On the **topology** axis (counting missing intra-batch edges) it is \(\theta\)=1.46 (95% CI \[1.33,1.59\]), with \(b=0.50\pm 0.04\); on the **recall** axis (the one the theorem needs) _a_<sub>recall</sub>=1.28 (95% CI \[1.03,1.52\]) at _N_<sub>0</sub>=100K, and a \(\mu\)-matched three- base fit gives _a_<sub>recall</sub>=1.45. Both place the exponent above 1 (super-linear) while individual CIs are wide, so the design rests on the sign, not the value (§III-A). The fit is valid over \(0.05\le c/N\le 0.45\); below _c/N_≈0.02 the per-merge loss falls under the 0.02 pp reporting floor and is excluded from every fit, so no claim is made for _c/N\<_0.05.

**Theorem 3** (Toy bound: anti-amortization)**.** _Under Poisson inserts-only arrivals and Assumption 2, over horizon T with_ \(M=\lceil\lambda_\mathrm{ins}T/c\rceil\) _merges whose per-merge losses assemble additively as an_ upper bound _(measurement finds the assembly subadditive,_ \(\eta<1\)_, so_ \(M\cdot g\) _over-states L_<sup>∗</sup>_; §V-B), and_ \(g(c,N)=\Theta(c^aN^{-b})\) _on the calibrated range_ \(0.05\le c/N\le 0.45\),

\(L^*(c,T)\le O\big(\lambda_\mathrm{ins}Tc^{a-1}N_0^{-b}\big),a-1\in[0.03,0.52]\) _(95% CI),_ \(\hat{a}-1\approx 0.28,\) (2)

_so this upper bound is_ non-decreasing _in the merge size c (strictly increasing on the point estimate) and L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_) _itself is measured non-decreasing directly (§V-B): the naive "batch bigger to amortize" (_\(L^*\propto 1/c\)_) is wrong in direction. Merge- induced degradation is_ irreducible by batching_, and each merge’s damage is capped by_ \(g\le c/(N+c)\)_, binding only as_ \(c\rightarrow N\).

## a) Scope of the toy bound.:

The central claim is the _sign:_ \(a\ge 1\), i.e. batching does not amortize. That sign forbids re- sizing merges as a recall lever, and it is supported by three fits on independent data (topology \(\theta\)=1.46, recall _a_=1.28 at fixed _N_<sub>0</sub>, \(\mu\)-matched recall _a_=1.45). The _magnitude_ is looser (_a_-1 could be as small as 0.03), so we rest the design on the sign, not the strength, of the super-linearity. Additive assembly is an assumption, and measurement finds it _conservative_, with twelve sequential merges at _c_=5000, _N_<sub>0</sub>=100K losing 0.38- 0.46 pp cumulatively against \(M\cdot g=1.04\) pp predicted (accumulation efficiency \(\eta\in[0.37,0.44]\)); _Mg_ thus over-states _L_<sup>∗</sup> in the conservative direction for an upper bound, though the constant is loose by \(2.3-2.7\times\). The _c_-dependence of _L_<sup>∗</sup> at horizon scale is instead _measured directly_ (§V-B(c)), where the twelve-merge run repeated across \(c\in\{1000,\dots,20000\}\) at a fixed 60K-insert horizon gives terminal recall monotonically decreasing in _c_, i.e. _L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_) monotonically _increasing_ (0.42<tbc>

<tbc>pp over a \(20\times\) range), so anti-amortization at horizon scale is a measurement rather than an extrapolation. The same five points also corroborate the _form_. With _a_-1=0.28 from the independent single-merge fit, _L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_)-_L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_<sub>min</sub>)=_A(c_<sup>_a_-1</sup>-_c_<sub>min</sub><sup>_a_-1</sup>) holds with _A_ constant to \(\pm 7\%\), whereas the _c<sup>a</sup>_ construction needs _A_ to move \(4.5\times\), so the 1_/c_ merge-count factor is measured, not assumed. The _c_-trend of \(\eta\) is reference- dependent and not pinned without a measured from-scratch 160K anchor, but neither the sub-additivity nor the measured _sign_ of _L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_) depends on that constant.

The consequence is the design principle of §IV: degradation cannot be reduced by re-sizing merges, only _re-prioritized_. Two mechanisms are isolated (Def. 1), M1 mutual invisibility (the super-linear driver, dominating \(c\unknown 0.1N\)) and a small _V_<sub>0</sub> hub-perturbation floor M2 (dominating \(c\lesssim 0.1N\)). A high- probability version also holds, since the _R_-cap gives _O(R_<sup>2</sup>) bounded influence per insert, so McDiarmid on the topology divergence and Bernstein on the (sparse, bounded) query loss give \(L^*\le\mathbb{E}[L^*](1+o(1))\) (proof in the supplementary material). Finally, small _c_ (recall-optimal) trades against tail latency (latency-optimal at large _c_: each merge inflates the tail for ≈_c/d_ seconds), the tension the scheduler navigates.

## b) The _V_<sub>0</sub> floor does not create an amortization regime.:

A natural objection: the floor _g_<sub>0</sub>(_L_) is _c_-independent, so paid once per merge it would contribute \(Mg_0=\lambda_\mathrm{ins}Tg_0/c\), _decreasing_ in _c_; adding it to the increasing batch term would produce an interior recall-optimal _c_<sup>∗</sup> and restore amortization at small _c_. Measurement settles it: over twelve merges the _V_<sub>0</sub> component _decays_ monotonically (\(4.80\rightarrow 3.43\rightarrow 2.51\rightarrow 1.38\) pp at _m_=1,4,8,12) rather than staying constant, and the cumulative loss is \(\checkmark Mg_0\). The floor is a saturating transient contributing _O_(1) rather than \(\Theta(M)\), so it generates no 1_/c_ term and _L_<sup>∗</sup>(_c_) has no interior optimum on the measured range. (The decomposition is scratch-free and not tie-aware, so its absolute magnitudes are confounded, but the conclusion rests only on the sign of the trend and the decomposition-free check \(L_\mathrm{cum}\checkmark Mg_0\).)

## c) Instantiating the constants.:

The \(\Theta(\cdot)\) hides constants we have measured, so the bound can be evaluated rather than merely asserted. On the calibrated range, with _g_ in recall points,

\(g(c,N)\approx 0.087(c/5000)^{1.28}(N/10^5)^{-0.64}\text{pp},L^*(c,T)\lesssim\big(\lambda_\mathrm{ins}T/c\big)g(c,N_0).\) (3)

Worked example: a tenant taking 10<sup>5</sup> inserts onto an _N_<sub>0</sub>=10<sup>5</sup> index at _c_=10<sup>4</sup> (_c/N_=0.1, inside range) sees _g_=0.21 pp per merge over _M_=10 merges, so \(L^*\le 2.1\) pp under additive assembly and ≈0.9 pp using the measured \(\eta\approx 0.4\); the per- merge cap _c/(N+c_)=0.091 is \(43\times\) slacker than the realized _g_<sub>frac</sub>=0.0021, so the cap is inactive, as it is everywhere below _c≈N_.

## B. The general theorem (C1-general): filtered, multi-tenant, deletes

Three assumptions lift the toy bound. The first formalizes local selectivity; the second is the modularity hinge; the third

<tbc>delimits the predicate class on which the filtered term is a _loss_ bound rather than a one-sided necessity statement.

**Assumption 4** (Local predicate density; the frontier is the post-filtered list)**.** \(\beta\) _is a property of the engine’s result contract, not a free constant:_ the post-filter can only see candidates the search returns, so \(\beta=1\) whenever the engine surfaces its full width-_L_ list to the filter (our disk post-filter path, and the measurement of §V-C, which post-filters a dump of exactly _L_ candidates), and \(\beta<1\) for an engine that truncates to _k_ before filtering. We take \(\beta=1\) throughout and carry \(\beta\) symbolically only so the law transfers to engines with a different contract. Filtered recall is governed by the local density \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(p,v)\), not the global \(\sigma(p)\): on the shared graph a width-_L_ greedy search returns a candidate frontier of effective size \(L_\mathrm{eff}=\beta L\) whose expected in-predicate mass is \(\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\).

**Assumption 5** (Per-merge degradation is filter and tenant-independent)**.** Because the disk graph is a single label-blind Yamana (§II), M_<sub>c</sub>_ and hence _g(c,N_) (Assumption 2) depend only on the label-agnostic vector set, not on the predicate or tenant partition.

**Assumption 6** (Per-query frontier model)**.** For a _single_ query _q_ with local density \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q)\), the in-predicate count of its frontier is \(X_q\sim\mathrm{Binom}(\beta L,\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q))\). This constrains one query’s neighborhood, not the query population: \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(\cdot)\) may vary arbitrarily across queries and tenants, and the tenant-level law is the _average of the per-query law over the query population_ (Lemma 7(iii)). Substituting a tenant’s _mean_ local density into the per-query law is a separate and strictly optimistic step, and spatially-clustered predicates break it (§V-C).

Assumption 5 makes the degradation term _transferable_ across the filter and tenant partition (the same _g(c,N_) applies regardless of predicate or tenant, i.e. modularity), rather than making the overall bound additive; the additivity of the two loss components is the separate union-bound argument of Theorem 8. It is measured: replaying the scheduler’s re-ordered multi-partition merge groupings to the identical terminal point set changes disk-graph recall by \(|\Delta|=0.02\) pp \(\le 0.67\) pp (§V), so merge re-ordering has negligible measured effect on terminal recall.

**Lemma 7** (Post-filter recall is a frontier-mass event)**.** _Fix a converged label-blind graph and a query q with local density_ \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q)\)_, and let X<sub>q</sub> be the in-predicate count of its frontier (Assumption 4). If the frontier is the true metric top-_\(\beta L\)_, then post-filter recall@k is_ exactly min(_X<sub>q</sub>,k)/k: the in- predicate members of a true top-_\(\beta L\) _list are precisely the nearest in-predicate points, so the first_ min(_X<sub>q</sub>,k_) _of them are ground-truth items (proof in the supplementary material). An approximate search can only_ omit _in-predicate ground- truth points that a true top-_\(\beta L\) _list would have contained, so the identity degrades in one direction: writing_ \(\delta_\mathrm{ann}(L)\) _for the expected fraction of a query’s in-predicate ground-truth points that lie in the true top-_\(\beta L\) _but are missed by the graph search,_ \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{recall}]\ge\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{min}(X_q,k)]/k-\delta_\mathrm{ann}(L)\)_. This is the_<tbc>

<tbc>_only direction Theorem 8 needs, since it bounds a recall_ loss _from above; the reverse inequality is not claimed. Then:_

(_i)_ (Assumption-free envelope; necessity.) _Without any distributional assumption on X,_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{min}(X,k)]/k\le\mathrm{min}\big(1,\frac{\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}}{k}\big),\) \(\text{(4)}\)

_so_ \(L\ge k/(\beta\sigma_\mathrm{loc})\) _is_ necessary _for recall_ \(\rightarrow 1\)_: recovery scale_ \(L=\Theta(k/\sigma_\mathrm{loc})\).<tbc>

(_ii)_ (Exact form under Assumption 6.) _With_ \(X\sim\mathrm{Binom}(\beta L,\sigma_\mathrm{loc})\)_, expected post-filter recall equals_<tbc>

\(h(\sigma_\mathrm{loc},L,k)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k\mathrm{Pr}\big[\mathrm{Binom}(\beta L,\sigma_\mathrm{loc})\ge i\big],\) \(\text{(5)}\)

_which_ \(\rightarrow 1\) _when_ \(\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\gg k\) _and_ \(\rightarrow\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}/k\) _when_ \(\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\checkmark k\)_. The single-term tail_ \(h_\mathrm{tail}=\mathrm{Pr}[\mathrm{Binom}(\beta L,\sigma_\mathrm{loc})\ge k]\) _is the i=k summand alone, so_ \(h_\mathrm{tail}\le h\le\mathrm{min}(1,\beta L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}/k)\)_: a tail-probability model is a valid but order-of-magnitude-loose lower bound on recall (§V-C)._<tbc>

(_iii)_ (Tenant law = query average; substituting the mean is optimistic.) _A tenant’s expected filtered recall is the_ average of the per-query law over its query population,<tbc>

\(\bar{h}_\tau(L,k)=\mathbb{E}_{q|\tau}\big[h(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q),L,k)\big],\) \(\text{(6)}\)

_and_ \(p\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{min}(\mathrm{Binom}(n,p),k)]\) _is concave in p, so by Jensen_<tbc>

\(\bar{h}_\tau(L,k)\le h\big(\mathbb{E}_{q|\tau}[\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q)],L,k\big):\) \(\text{(7)}\)

_plugging a tenant’s_ mean _local density into the per-query law over-predicts its recall, with a gap that grows with the dispersion of_ \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) _across queries and vanishes where h is linear (small x) or saturated (large x). Diffuse predicates have near-zero dispersion and are unaffected; spatially-clustered predicates are not, and §V-C exhibits the predicted curvature signature._<tbc>

_(iv)_ (Ordering.) _Collecting (i)-(iii),_ \(h_\mathrm{tail}\le\bar{h}_\tau\le h(\bar{\sigma}_\mathrm{loc}^{(\tau)},L,k)\le\mathrm{min}(1,\beta L\bar{\sigma}_\mathrm{loc}^{(\tau)}/k)\)_, so only the leftmost quantity is a lower bound on recall without further assumptions, and only the rightmost is an upper bound on recall without any._

_Status (§V-C):_ with \(\beta=1\) fixed by the engine contract (Assumption 4) and _no fitted constant of any kind_, part (ii) matches all 35 diffuse cells to a mean absolute residual of 0.2 pp (max 1.2 pp, two-sided), and predicts the separately-measured recovery constant \(L_{95}\approx 1.25k/\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) because _h_ crosses 0.95 at \(L\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\approx 1.25k\). On the clustered controls the residual is _uniformly one-signed_ (all 15 cells over-predict, up to +26 pp) and peaks in the knee _x_≈1-1.5, decaying to ≈1 pp at both ends. Two distinct clustering effects are at work. One is _density variation across queries_, where the dispersion of \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}(q)\) within a tenant makes the mean-substituted \(h(\bar{\sigma}_\mathrm{loc},L,k)\) optimistic by Jensen (Lemma 7(iii)); this is the curvature signature the +26 pp deficit exhibits, not a failure of the frontier- mass form. The other is _within-frontier correlation_, where spatially-clustered in-predicate points are not the independent<tbc>

**Theorem 8** (C1-general: per-tenant recall-bounded staleness)**.** _Under Assumptions 2, 4, 5, 6 with per-tenant insert rate_ \(\lambda_\mathrm{ins}^{(\tau)}\)_, local density_ \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}^{(\tau)}\)_, SLA staleness ceiling_ \(S_\tau\)_, and deletes/migration permitted, the worst-case (in t) per-tenant recall@k loss decomposes additively:_

## IV. SYSTEM: CACHE (C2) AND SCHEDULER (C3)

The two engineering contributions instantiate the theorem. C2 (the staging cache) absorbs within-cycle staleness on the query path so the loss the theorem bounds is the disk-graph term, not cache coverage; C3 (the scheduler) re-prioritizes background repair without ever re-sizing a merge, which is the only lever anti-amortization leaves. We prototype both on a FreshDiskANN fork with an `io\_uring` backend. _All numbers below are measured on this prototype unless marked otherwise._

### A. Substrate: one label-blind Yamana

The disk index is a _single_ Yamana graph over the label- agnostic vector set; predicates and tenant labels are query- time post-filter tags and never enter graph construction or the merge operator M_<sub>c</sub>_. Two properties follow, both central to §III. First, the per-merge degradation _g(c,N_) is _filter and tenant-independent_ (Assumption 5), the additivity hinge of Theorem 8. Second, a partition boundary can never induce topology degradation, because the graph never sees one; the scheduler’s re-ordering only changes which vectors co-merge and in what order. The prototype inherits the baseline’s merge exactly, and by design rather than by tuning: at every trigger all selected partitions are folded into _one_ combined in-memory index and handed to _one_ merge of size _c_, so the merge operator receives the same point set, at the same cadence, with the

<tbc>same Merge\_Size as the unmodified baseline. Partitioning is therefore invisible to M_<sub>c</sub>_ as a matter of code path, which is why the bound carries. We check that construction rather than infer it: with a single predicate and tenant the full C2+C3 prototype reproduces baseline post-merge recall@10 to \(\delta=0.000\) at three successive checkpoints (99.286/99.145/99.018, brute- force _K_=100 ground truth), with the ceiling-disabled, ceiling- never-firing, and FIFO legs byte-identical.

## B. C2: a filter-aware, tenant-aware staging cache

FreshDiskANN stages pending inserts in two in-memory buffers double-buffered against the disk merge. We re-key each buffer to a hash map over _partitions_ (_predicate,tenant_) and consult it on the query path, routing a query to its own partition and label-post-filtering disk results. The cache therefore serves freshly-inserted, same-tenant points immediately, which is what makes filtering on the query path viable and is essential for filtered queries, since disabling the query-path keying costs 72-86 pp of per-label recall@10 at live cache occupancy (93.8/78.9/81.1 keyed vs. 7.8/7.3/7.6 unkeyed, at comparable p99, with _identical_ probed staging occupancy in both legs so the staging state is held fixed). This ablation toggles more than a cache-probe comparison. A single query key drives both the cache probe and the disk post-filter, so the unkeyed leg is not a filter-blind cache alongside a correct disk path, since it pins every query’s key to one default partition, which simultaneously blinds the cache probe and points the disk post-filter at the wrong label for every tenant but one. The residual 7.5% is accordingly close to arithmetic, approximately the one correctly-keyed tenant’s share of the query mix times its recall. What the ablation establishes is that _the query-path keying as a whole_ is central; it does not measure a cache-probe-only lift. Isolating the probe would require holding the disk post-filter on the true label while blinding only the cache, which the current knobs do not expose; the tighter comparator (a filter-blind cache that post-filters its own contents) is therefore not measured. The cache changes only _what is staged and how queries route_, not the merge cadence; at a merge, all selected partitions are folded into _one_ combined in-memory index and drained as a _single_ merge of size _c_ (the combined-index single-merge drain), identical in topology to the baseline (merge-order parity \(\delta=0.000\)). This is what lets the bound carry to the prototype unchanged. Unlike read-side or filter-blind caches over vector indexes (Ubis, MicroNN, QVCache), ours is jointly filter and tenant-keyed, on the query path, and is the exact structure the theorem binds.

## C. C3: an SLA-aware, select-not-resize scheduler

The scheduler **never re-sizes a merge**; every fired merge is one combined fixed-size-_c_ drain (bound-safe by construction, §IV-A), and it wins by _selecting which pending work fills each merge and when_. The rule follows from Theorem 3, by which re-sizing is not a recall lever in the first place, so there is nothing to gain, and from holding the merge at the baseline’s shape, which keeps the bound applicable without re- deriving it per configuration. An implementation observation that draining _N_ partitions as _N_ separate merges reads much<tbc>

<tbc>worse (84.9/76.4/70.1) than the one-combined-merge design is _not_ used as evidence, since it holds nothing fixed, and the design rule rests on the two reasons above.

It orders background repair by a composite key

\(\kappa(w,t)=\alpha_1\mathrm{stale}(w,t)+\alpha_2\widehat{\Delta R}(w)+\alpha_3\mathrm{SLA}(w)+\alpha_4\mathrm{mig}(w),\) (9)

over staleness, predicted recall impact, tightest tenant SLA, and migration cost, each min-max normalized across the pending set at drain time. _Exactly one of these terms is exercised in every measurement we report_. The \(\widehat{\Delta R}\) term is implemented as an occupancy proxy behind a default-off flag and is disabled (\(\alpha_2=0\)) throughout, and no result depends on it. The migration term is identically zero in this prototype. The SLA term is inert whenever tenants share one SLO, since a term with a single distinct value normalizes to zero, and our churn legs additionally set \(\alpha_3=0\) so that ceiling enforcement is the only variable. So \(\kappa\) reduces to staleness ordering (oldest-first) in all reported runs; deferred units reload as the oldest across the driver’s per-merge restart and drain first. The four-term form is the interface the scheduler exposes, not a mechanism this paper validates; the measured win below comes from the ceiling.

On top of \(\kappa\), a **per-tenant max-taleness ceiling** \(S_\tau\) forcedrains a tenant whose staleness has reached \(S_\tau\). This is a _prioritization with a cadence-bounded overshoot_, and the distinction matters for Theorem 8. The built scheduler tests ceilings only at a merge trigger, with no early-merge on crossing, so a tenant that crosses \(S_\tau\) mid-window stays stale until the next trigger. The guarantee we actually deliver is

\(N_\tau^\mathrm{stale}\le\lambda_\mathrm{ins}^{(\tau)}\big(S_\tau+W\big),\) (10)

where _W_ is the trigger window (the high-water mark). The theorem’s \(\lambda_\mathrm{ins}^{(\tau)}S_\tau\) cap is thus the \(W\rightarrow 0\) idealization; the prototype attains it up to one window, and we set \(W=S_\tau^\mathrm{min}\) to make that overshoot as small as the design admits without an early-merge mechanism. The effect is directly visible in our runs, where a tight tenant’s measured staleness reaches 1900 against a 1000 ceiling before the force-drain resets it, and in an earlier configuration (even with _W_ set equal to \(S_\tau\), the tightest the built cadence allows) the tight tier was still violated at one checkpoint on _both_ legs for exactly this reason. Closing the gap would need an early-merge trigger. FIFO/threshold-triggered compaction (all prior streaming systems) has no per-tenant lever at all; §V-E shows the ceiling is what drives tight-tenant violations to zero under churn.

## D. Deletes and tenancy migration

Deletes are tombstoned in the staging partitions and evicted at the combined merge; a tenancy migration is a delete in \(\tau\) plus an insert in \(\tau'\). We extend the drain to evict tombstones from _every_ partition (not only a default one), verified to conserve points (zero silently-dropped) and to leave deleted ids absent from post-merge results while survivors remain. This is what admits the deletes/migration term of Theorem 8; the term’s precise floor contribution \(g_0^\mathrm{del}\) is not characterized here.

The general theorem’s additivity rests on the scheduler not degrading the terminal graph (Assumption 5). ### F. Baselines and Curator: the tradeoff on static data

On static low-per-tenant data (_T_=6\(\rightarrow\)96, fixed total _N_), per-tenant sharding is _not_ navigability-limited (shards recall ≈100) but is _memory_-limited, its summed footprint growing linearly in tenant count and OOMing a 3 GB box at _T_=96 (FreshDiskANN-shard \(393\rightarrow\)6144 MB, PipeANN- shard \(757\rightarrow\)11776 MB), whereas our shared graph is flat. Under matched search cost our post-filter recall degrades with tenant count (the \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) effect, §V-C). Our Curator comparison uses the authors’ published artifact at a pinned commit, so it measures genuine per-tenant navigability rather than a post- filter over a label-blind graph. It recalls ≈100 flat at ∼100 MB in-memory and thus beats us on _static_ recall; our contribution is instead on streaming, per-tenant SLA scheduling, the bound and disk-resident scale, axes the evaluated static, in-memory Curator artifact does not target. The outcome on static data is a _tradeoff_, not a clean win for either side; the payoff axis is churn (§V-E) and scale (§V-G).

At 100K our prototype runs _bounded_ (steady RSS ≈1.06 GB single-tenant, ≈1.67 GB six-tenant) and _correct_ (recall@10 99.70, on-curve), with the SLA win intact, closing<tbc>

Because in-memory footprints are \(\propto N\) while a disk-resident index keeps the graph and full-precision vectors on disk, the memory picture should _invert_ at scale, since an in-memory Curator at its measured 5.6 KB/vector exceeds 16 GB by ≈2.9M points and needs ≈56 GB at 10M, whereas only the PQ-compressed vectors and tags (32-128 B/vector) grow with _N_ on our side, putting us at ≈1-2 GB even at 10M.

_The scaling claim rests on a decomposition, not on the two headline RSS points, which conflate several quantities._ An RSS breakdown at fixed tenant and thread count (_T_=6, 32 threads) on the matched 18K/100K pair separates three marginals. The _serving_ graph-residency marginal is **0.115 kB/point** (PQ codes and tags resident in RAM, the graph on disk), matching the PQ-code size architecturally (≈102 B/point at 100K); serving memory is therefore _N_-independent up to that marginal and the bounded-memory claim holds _for serving_. The _merge-peak transient_ is **8.3 kB/point**, incurred while the StreamingMerger rewrites the _O(N_) graph in RAM under 32 build threads and released afterwards (proportional to _N_, reducible by thread and batch configuration). Between the two sits the _whole- process first stable RSS_, which grows at ≈2.6 kB/point on the matched pair, above the serving marginal because it includes configured allocations (per-thread search buffers, staging sized as #partitions \(\times 2\)Merge\_Size) that the supplementary RSS decomposition (Fig. S3) does not fully attribute to _N_; isolating that residual is left open. This decomposition supersedes an earlier reading that took the raw two-point 18K\(\rightarrow\)100K RSS slope (≈10 kB/point) at face value and extrapolated it to ≈11 GB at 1M. That slope is the mixed whole-process quantity, not a serving cost, which is why the 1M-10M rows in  IV are quoted as residency-model _projections_ on the 0.115 kB/point serving term rather than as extrapolations of the raw curve. The 0.115 kB/point marginal is a two-point measurement whose agreement with the PQ-code size makes it credible.

Where per-query densities are unavailable, the assumption-free envelope Lemma 7(i) constrains the required search width but gives no per-tenant recall guarantee. _d) Scale and measurement scope.:_ The SLA _mechanism_ is measured (ceiling enforcement drives tight-tier violations to zero under churn where a scheduler-less baseline cannot) and the shard rebuild-outage is measured to 100K/tenant, but the shard violation _rate_ is a duty-cycle model and the 1M-10M memory inversion is a projection from measured per-vector RSS. The topology-\(\Delta\) is a same-method _relative_ measurement with limited power to exclude sub-pp differences, and our absolute _p_99 trails PipeANN’s by roughly an order of magnitude at the configurations measured; external comparisons are preliminary (the PipeANN recall gap is on unmatched parameters; ACORN did not build within our memory ceiling). Results are on a single dataset family (SIFT and a filtered YFCC slice) and a single storage backend, so the measured constants may not transfer to other datasets or storage stacks without recalibration. Finally, the analysis presupposes a merge-based (out-of-place) substrate; direct- insert indexes have no _c/d_/\(\tau\) referent and lie outside our scope. ## VIII. CONCLUSION We studied the intersection of graph-substrate, filtered, multi-tenant, streaming ANN with an analytical per-tenant recall@_k_ bound, which prior work has not jointly addressed. The organizing result is anti-amortization, and we observe it directly: over a fixed 60K-insert horizon and a \(20\times\) range of merge sizes, terminal recall falls monotonically as merges grow. On this substrate, batching is therefore not a free recall- amortization lever; degradation can be re-prioritized but not amortized away. The per-merge law behind it is super-linear in _c_ across the evaluated _c/N_ range, with an exponent estimated from that range rather than derived. That fact explains the design: a filter and tenant-aware staging cache that absorbs within-cycle staleness on the query path (C2), and a select- not-resize, SLA-aware scheduler that re-orders repair under a per-tenant max-staleness ceiling (C3), both binding to a bound we generalize to the filtered (local-density \(\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\)), multi- tenant (cadence-bounded), deletes/migration setting (C1). The filtered half of that bound is a parameter-free frontier-mass law (expected in-predicate frontier mass truncated at _k_) that predicts the measured recovery scale \(L_{95}=1.25k/\sigma_\mathrm{loc}\) and holds as a loss bound under homogeneous local density. On a FreshDiskANN substrate we measure that the scheduler’s re-ordering leaves terminal recall unchanged, that the per- tenant staleness ceiling eliminates tight-tier violations under churn where a scheduler-less baseline cannot, and that the design stays memory-bounded and recall-correct at mid-scale. PipeANN and OdinANN remain stronger on single-tenant recall and tail latency, and Curator on static filtered recall; our contribution targets the filtered, multi-tenant, streaming axes and the per-tenant freshness guarantee. ## REFERENCES
